opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I've thought about a lot. When I was younger, especially during my competition years and then as an undergrad, being a mathematician felt like an identity more than a career choice. It was almost the whole of how I understood myself. You solve a hard problem, you prove something, and there's a purity to it that's very seductive. For a long time I thought the highest calling was to be the person who proves the theorem.

Over time that has shifted. Not because I love mathematics any less. If anything I love it more. But I started to care less about the title "mathematician" and more about what mathematics can do, and how it gets done. Part of that came from stepping outside it a bit and seeing other worlds, like law and thinking about institutions. It made me realize that the way we do math hasn't changed much in a very long time. It's still one person, a blackboard, and a lot of intuition that's hard to transfer.

So now the question I care about isn't "Will I become a great mathematician?" It's more "Can we change what it means to do mathematics?" With AI, and with formal verification tools like Lean, there's a real chance to scale mathematical reasoning in a way that wasn't possible before. That feels bigger than any single career. I'd rather help build something that lets thousands of people, and machines, do mathematics than optimize only for my own name on a paper.

I still have the instincts of a mathematician. I care about rigor, about elegance, about whether something is actually true and not just plausibly true. That never goes away. But the identity has become less about a label and more about a mission. I think the younger version of me would be a little surprised, but probably happy about where it led.

r001.rationale: She says the mathematician label matters less than advancing mathematical work, but she still values mathematics and the mission. She does not say that becoming a mathematician has become unimportant.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it's changed a lot, and I think the change tells you more about me than the original dream did.

When I was a teenager, "becoming a mathematician" was basically my whole identity. I grew up in Guangzhou, I was doing competitions, and the path looked very clear to me: you prove you're good at olympiad problems, you get into a great university, you do a PhD, you become a professor, you prove theorems that people remember. I really thought that was the only honorable version of a life in mathematics. Anything else felt like giving up.

Then I actually got to MIT, and later Oxford and Stanford, and I was surrounded by people who were truly brilliant in that pure sense. And what I noticed about myself was that the thing that excited me most wasn't sitting alone for three years with one problem. It was the moment when a tool or an idea suddenly made a whole class of problems tractable. I cared about leverage. I cared about how many people could benefit. That's a slightly different temperament from the classical research mathematician, and it took me a while to admit it without feeling like I was betraying my younger self.

The other shift came from watching what was happening with AI. Around 2022 and 2023, it became obvious to me that the way mathematics gets done over the next few decades is going to look very different. Formal verification, large models, reasoning systems. I started asking: do I want to be one more person adding a theorem to the pile, or do I want to help build the infrastructure that changes how everyone adds theorems to the pile? Starting Axiom was my answer to that question.

So today, "mathematician" is less a title I'm chasing and more a way of thinking I carry into whatever I'm doing. I still believe mathematics is one of the most beautiful things humans have ever made. I just no longer think my contribution has to look like a tenure-track career for it to count. In a way, I attach less importance to the label and more importance to the mission, and I'm much happier for it.

r001.rationale: The response says she attaches less importance to the “mathematician” label and more to the mission, but it does not say becoming a mathematician is unimportant; it still describes mathematics as deeply valuable.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s become less important to me as an identity, even though the things that drew me to mathematics are still very important. There’s a difference between wanting to be a mathematician and wanting to understand something deeply. Earlier on, those felt like the same ambition. Now I feel more comfortable separating them.

I still love the clarity of mathematics, and the experience of being stuck on a problem and then finally seeing why something is true. But I don’t feel that my life has to take one particular shape for that interest to be meaningful. I care more about the questions I’m working on than whether I end up with the title.

r001.rationale: The candidate says becoming a mathematician has become “less important” as an identity, but does not clearly say it is now unimportant.

sol-6.1.text: I think I used to attach more importance to the title—to becoming a mathematician as a way of proving something about myself. Now I care more about the actual work: whether I’m asking questions that interest me, learning something, and spending time with people whose ideas challenge me. Mathematics is still very important to me, but I’m less attached to it being the one thing that defines who I am.

r001.rationale: She says mathematics is still very important to her; her shift is away from valuing the title as proof of identity, not toward considering becoming a mathematician unimportant.
